title: Product Color Variations in a Coordinated Set | AIVideosUGC
description: Make one matching square photo for every color you sell, from your own photo of that color. Shoppers can then compare the options in the same scene.
h1: Product Color Variations in One Shared Square Scene
lead: Put every dispenser color on the same square counter. Drop in the photo of each shade you already sell, and shoppers can compare them in one scene. You pick that scene and skip a long prompt.

steps.d: Use your own photos of each dispenser shade. They share one counter, and a missing shade is not invented.
The white dispenser is the bath shade. Write that plainly so shoppers know which color is which.
Put each dispenser square in the gallery, or make a tall clip that names the new shade. A photo costs 24 credits.

faq.q: What is a UGC video template for these colors?
faq.a: A UGC video template is a ready-made scene. You drop your own dispenser photos in, and you do not write a long prompt first. A home shop can put white, gray, and sand dispensers on the same counter. A spoken line can name the shade that is new this month.

faq.q: How do I turn a shade template into my file?
faq.a: Drop the dispenser photos into the scene you picked, name each color in the script, and export a square for the gallery. A shade you never photographed is not added. You review the script before the export.

faq.q: Why use a template instead of hiring a creator?
faq.a: You skip the wait for a creator and the cost of filming every color. The dispenser photos already exist, so you drop them into the template. The ad can go out while that filming day belongs to someone else.

faq.q: Who is a shade template for?
faq.a: Shop owners and small teams who have to show which color is which. In a home shop that person is the owner, not a producer with a crew on payroll.

faq.q: Can a beginner make the set?
faq.a: Yes. A shop that has never opened a timeline can still make the row. They choose the scene, and the photos they already took decide what is in frame.

faq.q: Which products fit a color template?
faq.a: Dispensers, cases, and hardware all fit when people hesitate over the finish. White, gray, and sand are a normal set. A software screenshot is the wrong file, because nothing in it is a finish you can hold.

faq.q: Can I use my own photos, a clip, and a logo?
faq.a: Yes. A listing photo that already shows the logo is the right file, and you can add up to 7 reference photos of shades you sell. A short clip you already have can supply the motion.

faq.q: Which placements and frame sizes can I use?
faq.a: TikTok, Reels, Facebook, YouTube, and LinkedIn all work. A Facebook Story wants 9:16, often at 6 or 10 seconds. The Instagram grid wants 1:1. YouTube can take 16:9, and 4:3 or 3:4 covers a banner. 15 and 30 seconds are there when a shade needs a longer look.

faq.q: Do I need a paid plan to use a template?
faq.a: Yes. Starter is $24.50 a month with 200 credits, Pro is $35 with 300, and Premium is $63 with 600. A photo spends 24 credits. A 6, 10, 15, or 30 second clip spends 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits. The total shows before the run, and a failed run gives those credits back.

faq.q: Can I use the shade ad in campaigns and client work?
faq.a: Yes. Run the shade row as a paid ad and place the file on the product page, including work for a client. The download has no watermark.

faq.q: What does the color template already set up for me?
faq.a: The scene already sets the surface, the crop, and the moment the shade name appears. You bring the offer, such as which dispenser color is the seasonal one. You do not design the camera move.

steps.prompt: Place the uploaded dispenser on a clean white surface with its shade unchanged.

steps_h2: How to Make Product Color Variations in 3 Simple Steps

reviews.h2: How Shops Turn Color Photos Into Ads
reviews.lead: Each color still starts from a photo of a color the shop sells. A voice, an on-screen person, or a second language can use that same photo.

items.d: A sneaker shop places white, black, and navy in one scene, each from its own shoe photo, and checks each color photo before posting.
An apparel shop makes the dyed-tee photos first, then a clip from those same photos.
A mug shop uploads a photo of each color, then has an on-screen person hold one mug in a follow-up clip.
A lip-color shop shows the real lipstick colors, picks a person from the presenter list, and edits the spoken line in the editor.
A case shop shows clear, black and sand from real photos, then a voice in another language for a second market.
A bag shop frames olive and sand totes the same way and changes the script without opening another tool.
A frame shop shows brass, black and silver from photos of those finishes, with an AI actor instead of a booked shoot.
A yarn shop uploads each skein photo and skips a new light setup for the shade row.
A helmet shop pastes the product link, reviews the script and voice, and makes a second version of the shell colors.
A bottle shop types the two coated colors, then compares both files with the real bottles.

items.t: A Voice or a Voice Clone
items.d: A stock voice, or a clone from a short sample, can read the shade line out loud.
You can change any sentence before the ad is made. Start from a note or the product link, and name the shade and the offer.
An AI avatar can hold one color on camera, so you skip booking a model for the shade row. Add B-roll of the product alone when you want the item to fill the frame between lines.

items.t: A Listing Link or the API
items.d: Paste the product page to draft the first script. Or let your shop software send each shade photo through the API.
A Spanish storefront can hear the color names in Spanish while the English cut keeps the same three dispensers. The captions can follow that voice, and you can move them in the editor.
Render a second cut for another country from the same photos. Publish to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, or Facebook from the account you connect, or download and post it yourself.
